technique: withholding — what the poem refuses to name or explain, and why that works
lesson:
Today we work on one thing: withholding. That means the poem keeps back a word or a fact on purpose, so you feel the gap where it should be.

Look at what the poem will not name. "Nothing out there finishes itself." It never says who left the work undone. "the maul leaned where you left it"—it never says when, or why you walked off. "each one a small plain promise you mean to keep"—it names the clove but not the worry behind it.

Here is why it works. When the poem skips the reason, your mind fills it in. You supply the guilt about the unfinished shed. You supply the pressure of the coming frost. What you add yourself hits harder than anything the poem could tell you outright.

Try this: write the scene, then cross out the one line that explains the feeling. Leave only the object and the task.

The second time through, listen for how much never gets explained before the poem says "So — up!"

Here is the poem.
poem:
The woodshed stands part-stacked, a cord and a half
split and the rest still rounds, pale-faced in the leaves,
the maul leaned where you left it with the handle gone to dew.
Nothing out there finishes itself. The fence sags
at the low corner, half-mended, waiting on a staple
and the patience to set it right instead of fast.
On the bench, the cloves wait in their loose white heap,
more than a man can rightly number by the eye—
each one a small plain promise you mean to keep in the ground
before the first real frost locks the beds for good.
The light's come up now, thin and honest on the rows,
and it asks nothing of you but what your two hands ask:

Something's half-finished and waiting for your hands—better to meet it awake than let it keep till noon—

So — up!
